cues.text: A Mother Chosen Twice

Born Zoé Labouré on 2 May 1806 at Fain-lès-Moutiers in Burgundy, the ninth of eleven surviving children of a prosperous farmer and his devout wife, Catherine lost her mother, Madeleine, when she was only nine years old.
Returning from the funeral, she is remembered as having taken up a small statue of Our Lady from the family mantel and held it close.
She said, "Now, dear Blessed Virgin, you will be my mother."
This child's vow would prove, in the end, no passing grief but the whole shape of a life.
A Farmhouse, Not a Schoolroom
With her mother gone and her older sisters married or already in religious life, the household fell to Catherine.
At only twelve, she took charge of her father's farm kitchen and its brood of younger siblings, receiving almost no formal schooling in the years that followed.
When she confided at eighteen that she wished to enter the convent, her father refused outright.
He sent her instead to work as a waitress in an uncle's café in Paris, hoping the city's distractions would quiet a vocation he could not understand.
The scheme failed entirely.
Catherine remained as set on religious life amid the noise of the café as she had been in her father's quiet kitchen, and an aunt's steady intercession eventually won her father's reluctant consent.
A Priest Seen Before He Was Known
Some years before that consent came, Catherine reported a vivid dream of an elderly priest beckoning her toward a room full of the sick, telling her, "It is a good deed to look after the sick.
God has designs on you; do not forget it."
She recognized his face only later, and by surprise, in a portrait hanging on the wall of a Daughters of Charity hospital.
It was St. Vincent de Paul , dead for over a century and a half, whose own daughters she would soon join.
In January 1830, at twenty-three, Catherine entered the novitiate of the Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul .
That April, she arrived at the community's motherhouse on the Rue du Bac in Paris.
It was the very convent where, within months, her hidden life would be interrupted by visions no one could have prepared her for.
The Virgin in the Motherhouse Chapel
On the night of 18–19 July 1830, a child's voice woke Catherine and led her to the convent chapel.
There, she found the Blessed Virgin seated near the sanctuary and kept vigil at her feet for hours, hearing a warning of coming trials for France and for the Church.
That warning seemed, within days, confirmed by the revolution that broke out across Paris that same July.
On 27 November of that same year, in the same chapel, Mary appeared to her again, standing on a globe.

Rays of light streamed from her hands, framed by an oval bearing the words "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee," and instructed Catherine to have a medal struck to this exact design.
Catherine herself never sought to explain why she, of all the sisters at Rue du Bac, had been chosen for so extraordinary a grace.
She simply did as she had been told, and trusted the rest to obedience.
A Medal, and a Silence Kept for Life

Catherine confided everything to her confessor, the Vincentian priest Fr. Jean-Marie Aladel , who doubted her account for nearly two years before finally seeking the Archbishop of Paris's permission to have the medal struck in 1832.
What became known almost at once as the Miraculous Medal spread across France and then the world with extraordinary speed.
Within its first years, it was credited with a great many reported healings and conversions.
Yet Catherine herself asked that her own identity as the visionary be kept secret, and Fr. Aladel honored that request until shortly before his own death.
Appointed after her formation to the community's hospice at Enghien-Reuilly , on the edge of Paris, Catherine spent the remaining forty-six years of her religious life there in unbroken obscurity.
She tended the elderly and infirm, kept the poultry yard, and answered the convent gate, known to her own sisters only as a quiet, faithful, rather unremarkable member of the community.
Not even the superior who worked alongside her for years suspected that the humble portress beside her had once kept vigil at Our Lady's own feet.
Legacy
Only in the final months of her life, in 1876, did Catherine finally reveal her secret.
She told her superior plainly that she believed she would not live to see another Christmas and that the truth could not be buried with her.
She died at Enghien-Reuilly on 31 December 1876, seventy years old.
When her body was exhumed in 1933 during her cause for canonization, it was found remarkably incorrupt.
It still rests beneath the same chapel on the Rue du Bac, where she had once knelt before the Virgin as an anonymous young novice.

Beatified in 1933 and canonized in 1947 by Pope Pius XII, Catherine Labouré is remembered by the Church less for her visions’ brilliance than for the forty-six ordinary, hidden years that followed them.
Her life helped prepare the ground for the definition of the Immaculate Conception in 1854 and, in time, for Lourdes itself.
It still says to every believer tempted to think their hidden faithfulness goes unnoticed: it does not.
